narrative:
The model determined that you have an 82% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were by far the strongest reasons for the negative prediction. In both years you placed in the bottom decile of your class, far below the average of roughly the sixth and fifth deciles among students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings strongly pushed the model toward expecting bar exam failure. Your LSAT score of 35 was the third most important factor; while it pulled the prediction slightly in a more positive direction, the improvement was not nearly enough to offset the effect of your class standing.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.9, middle-income background, full-time study plans, gender, and race played little or no role in the outcome. The system focused almost entirely on how your grades compared with those of your classmates.

To improve your chances, you should consider retaking the LSAT and aiming for a noticeably higher score, or strengthening your academic record through additional coursework that demonstrates consistent high performance. These steps would directly address the factors that most hurt your current prediction. (218 words)
